title: Justin describes the Mass (c. 155)
hookLine: a philosopher writes to the emperor about Sunday: readings, prayers, bread and wine, a collection for the poor

cards: The letter is addressed to the emperor of Rome, and the man writing it wears a philosopher's cloak. His name is Justin.

He looked for the truth among the philosophers, one school after another, found Christ, and kept the cloak. Rumors about Christians are going around: secret meetings, strange meals, who knows what behind closed doors.
Justin could simply ask for mercy. He does something bolder. He tells the emperor exactly what Christians do on Sunday, step by step.

teach.b: Justin is called an apologist. That doesn't mean he said sorry. In the Greek of the first letter of Peter, the answer Christians should be ready to give is an apologia, a defense.
The Douay-Rheims puts it: ready to give "a reason of that hope which is in you." An apologist gives that reason to people outside. Justin's reason is a plain description.

On the day called Sunday, he writes, people from the city and the countryside gather in one place. The memoirs of the apostles, his name for the Gospels, or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time allows.
Then the one presiding speaks, urging everyone to imitate these good things. All stand and pray.

teach.h: BREAD, WINE AND WATER, THEN AMEN.
teach.b: Bread is brought, and wine mixed with water. The presider offers prayers and thanksgiving, and the people answer: Amen. The deacons give each person a share, and carry some to those who are absent.
Then the collection: those who have plenty, and are willing, give what each thinks fit. The presider uses it for orphans and widows, the sick, prisoners, and strangers passing through.

Justin even explains the day: Sunday is when God began making the world, and when Jesus rose from the dead. And Christians, he says, don't receive this food as common bread and common drink. They call it the Eucharist.
The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes this passage at length.
It dates it around the year 155, and says the basic lines of the celebration have stayed the same until our own day: readings, a homily, prayers, the gifts, the great Amen, communion.

how: At Mass, Catholics hear readings and a homily (the Liturgy of the Word), then the gifts are brought forward and the Eucharistic prayer ends in the great Amen before communion (the Liturgy of the Eucharist); parishes usually take a collection as well.

o: someone who gives a reasoned defense of the faith
someone who apologizes for the Church's wrongs
a monk who copies out the writings of saints

p: carry a share to the absent

s: an apologist is someone who says sorry for the faith
apologia means a defense: a reason given to people outside.
Justin says Christians don't receive the bread and cup as common food
he says they call this food the Eucharist.
Justin says Christians met in secret on a weekday night
he says they gathered on the day called Sunday, the day of creation and of the resurrection.

games.q: you're Justin. rumors about Christian meetings are spreading, and you're writing to the emperor. what goes in the letter?
o: ask for mercy and say nothing more.
describe exactly what happens on Sunday.
games.why: Justin lays out the whole Sunday: readings, preaching, prayers, bread and wine, the Amen, a collection for the poor. the plain description was his defense.

practice: Walk back through the last Mass you were at, or one you've seen: the readings, the preaching, everyone standing to pray, bread and wine carried forward, the Amen, communion, the basket going down the row.
Lay Justin's Sunday over it and notice where they line up; if you've never been, hold the picture of a room of ordinary people doing these few things together. If you pray, say one quiet Amen.

wordCard.voice: Apologist. Someone who gives a defense of the faith, a reason, to people outside it, the way Justin did. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: defense — the word in 1 Peter 3:15 for the reason Christians give.

carryVoice: Your line: the same Mass. From the Didache to Justin, the first Christians, in their own words. See you tomorrow.
